posture: One NSW item, and it lands squarely on delegation risk: SIRA has now put on the record, twice, that handing claims to an administrator does not hand over the licence obligations that come with them.

items.headline: SIRA rejects the administrator-transition excuse, putting every self-insurer claims handover on notice
items.summary: Insurance Business Australia analysed SIRA's August censure of Aldi Stores under section 183A(1)(b) of the Workers Compensation Act 1987, reporting that the regulator refused to accept Aldi's argument that its non-conformances arose around a change of third-party administrator, and held instead that using a claims manager does not displace the self-insurer's own licence obligations. The piece sets that alongside a separate SIRA audit of the QBE Treasury Managed Fund claims handover, which found high case-manager turnover and documented handover records on only a small minority of transferred claims, and notes that 37 remediation plans across the workers compensation sector remained open at 31 March 2026.
items.so_what: Two audits of two unrelated entities produced the same conclusion, which turns a one-off censure into a stated regulatory position: outsourcing claims administration transfers the work but not the accountability, and a transition period is treated as a risk the licensee was obliged to manage rather than an excuse. Any NSW self-insurer mid-way through or planning a TPA change should be testing continuity of compliance, case management and data quality now, because a high-risk rating on any single audit component triggers a remediation plan — and Aldi's own September self-audit is the near-term test of how hard SIRA intends to press.
